entries.title: Trevon Williams brings the energy as Ag. Science beats Goode to win the Red Southwest
entries.summary: <p>The opening kickoff of a high school football game is rarely notable, but <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/10/08/high-school-football-scores-week-8" >Thursday</a> at Goode it was a preview of what was to come in a conference championship-deciding game between Ag. Science and the host Knights.</p><p>Ag. Science senior Trevon Williams burst past every player on the field and flattened Goode’s kick returner, setting the tone for the Cyclones’ 31-24 win.</p><p>“He’s been like that since he was a freshman,” Ag. Science coach Pat Ade said. “He started as a freshman and was quiet the first two years. He’s a lot more vocal now. He means so much to this team. He is definitely one of our big-time leaders.”</p><p>Williams caught a 14-yard touchdown pass in the first quarter and had five catches for 98 yards, while also playing a key defensive role in slowing down Goode’s high-powered rushing attack.</p><p>“Every game I try to bring the most energy I can and lift my team up,” Williams said.</p><p>Goode (5-2, 4-1) turned the ball over to Ag. Science on fumbles on its first three possessions and trailed 19-0 in the first quarter.</p><p>But the Knights charged back. Aedan Cleveland’s 36-yard TD run midway through the third quarter cut Ag. Science’s lead to 19-18. Then Goode cut the deficit to one point again with 9:31 left when Gabriel Chambers-Crosby got loose for a 50-yard touchdown run.</p><p>“They locked in and got focused,” Knights coach Terrence McClarn said. “A lot of teams would have crumbled, but our guys pulled it together. We have to work on our mistakes and eliminate those fumbles.”</p><p>Ag. Science (7-1, 4-0) sealed the win with an 11-yard touchdown run by James Gregory with 6:55 left, followed by a couple of big defensive stops.</p><p>“Trying to keep up with [Goode’s] run game is something we have been worried about all season,” Ade said. “They just do a heck of a job. We changed it up after halftime, and kind of slowed it down. They went back to the middle stuff and changed it up again.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b00000" name="image-b00000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dd43766/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+39/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F42%2Ff8%2F55cc581b41c8aa1c77dc66e3b9e5%2Fob-cst-091026-7009.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9ded617/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+39/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F42%2Ff8%2F55cc581b41c8aa1c77dc66e3b9e5%2Fob-cst-091026-7009.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c715f11/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+39/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F42%2Ff8%2F55cc581b41c8aa1c77dc66e3b9e5%2Fob-cst-091026-7009.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ag. entries.title: Hundreds of Lincoln Park High School students walk out in solidarity with Jane Doe in Cornell rape case
entries.summary: <p>Several hundreds of students walked out of Lincoln Park High School on Thursday afternoon in solidarity with Jane Doe, the former Cornell University student who alleged she was raped by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity at the Ivy League school in 2024.</p><p>The case has drawn widespread attention after <a class="Link" href="https://www.cornellsun.com/article/2026/09/tccsuykuvb4z" target="_blank" >the woman filed a lawsuit against Cornell</a> and the seven men accused of raping her. In the lawsuit, she alleges Cornell took insufficient action in response to her initial allegations. The woman filed as "Jane Doe," common in lawsuits where the accuser doesn't want their name made public.</p><p>The crowd stretched several blocks as students marched from Oz Park through the Lincoln Park neighborhood. Students chanted “No means no” throughout the walk and held signs declaring “Women’s rights are human rights,” “Intoxication is not an invitation,” and “If it’s not yes, it’s no.”</p><p>Key organizers of the walkout, Isabella Scaffai and Elianna St.Martin, were among the seniors leading the march, while several students gave short speeches throughout the walk. (Scaffai is the daughter of a staff member at WBEZ.)</p><p>St.Martin, 17, said the walkout was organized Thursday in support of student walkouts taking place nationally the same day.</p><p>“We just want to be a part of that and show our support for all the Jane Does around the world because more people need to speak out about these issues because just staying silent isn’t going to bring the change that we want to happen,” St.Martin said.</p><p>Several other students also spoke about sexual violence and standing in solidarity with friends and loved ones who had experienced sexual assault.</p><p>Senior Laila Sharda, 17, said the case has made her more critical of Ivy League universities and prompted her to rethink where she wants to attend college.</p><p>“It is such an abomination that these Ivy League schools think that they can pay their way out of real issues,” Sharda said. “I want to make sure that I'm in a college that respects me and respects my boundaries."</p><p>Sharda had also been keen on joining Greek life at university, but said the case has made her increasingly skeptical of fraternities and sororities.</p><p>Senior Luis Torres, 17, said he believes several of the “Cornell 7” weren't punished enough by the university.</p><p>“It’s completely unjustified how people at Cornell University only had the audacity to just expel two of their kids and make the others write essays,” Torres said. “I find that completely unbelievable.”</p><p>Near the end of the march, several students began chanting, “My body,” with the crowd responding, “My choice.”</p><p>“We are all Jane Does until no one is Jane Doe,” Scaffai told the crowd.</p>

entries.title: Judge threatens to order Midway Blitz agents to hand over personal phones — after Bovino refused
entries.summary: <p>A federal judge in Chicago warned the Trump administration Thursday that any Homeland Security employee<b> </b>who worked Operation Midway Blitz might be ordered to turn over their personal phones for review — if litigation over the deportation campaign moves forward.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Sara<b> </b>Ellis<b> </b>did not explicitly order the phones be turned over. She <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz/2026/09/02/federal-judge-told-things-are-no-longer-quiet-as-midway-blitz-lawsuit-faces-critical-november-ruling" target="_blank" >has yet to rule</a> on whether she will even let the lawsuit move forward. But she told a Justice Department attorney she expects the government to make her intentions known, so data is not lost.</p><p>“It’s clear to me that agents were using their personal phones for work communication,” Ellis said. “And what I won’t allow to happen … is for people to hide behind saying that ‘these are our personal phones,’ when they are being used as work phones.”</p><p>Such an order would likely meet a significant challenge from the Trump administration. A government lawyer warned her that a similar order already met resistance in California, where<b> </b>the feds unleashed Operation At Large<b> </b>before turning their attention to Chicago.</p><p>Ellis has gone head-to-head with Midway Blitz officials before, though, even ordering<b> </b>then-U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/24/federal-judge-orders-border-patrol-commander-greg-bovino-into-her-courtroom" target="_blank" >into her courtroom</a><b> </b>last October. She referenced her experience with Bovino on Thursday, noting that “I have a hard time crediting what Mr. Bovino says.”</p><p>“It’s documented that he has a hard time telling the truth,”<b> </b>Ellis said. “Even when he’s under oath.”</p><p>Ellis presides over the lawsuit brought by Illinois and Chicago against Homeland Security. It alleges Midway Blitz was designed to coerce the state and city into assisting the federal government with its aggressive deportation efforts.</p><p>Ellis is set to rule Nov. 17 on Homeland Security’s bid to have the lawsuit tossed out.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz/2026/09/02/federal-judge-told-things-are-no-longer-quiet-as-midway-blitz-lawsuit-faces-critical-november-ruling" >Federal judge told ‘things are no longer quiet’ as Midway Blitz lawsuit faces critical November ruling</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Last fall, Ellis handled separate litigation over the feds’ use of force during Midway Blitz. That’s how she wound up ordering Bovino into her courtroom. She tried to force him to appear regularly in her courtroom, over the course of a week, to discuss his agents’ actions.</p><p>The federal appeals court in Chicago<b> </b>intervened, insisting the move <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/31/bovinos-daily-meetings-with-judge-would-infringe-on-separation-of-powers-appeals-court-says" target="_blank" >violated the separation of powers</a> between the courts and the executive branch. The appeals court also vacated<b> </b>a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >preliminary injunction</a> Ellis<b> </b>later<b> </b>handed down, which governed the agents’ use of force.</p><p>That litigation largely came to an end<b> </b>in January.</p><p>But Thursday, Ellis met with lawyers to discuss evidence in the new lawsuit brought by Illinois and Chicago. Among other things, Justice Department attorneys<b> </b>Lee Reeves and<b> </b>Jonathan<b> </b>Robbins explained efforts to preserve data from Bovino’s work and personal phones following Bovino’s retirement last spring.</p><p>Bovino<b> </b>reported<b> </b>a work phone as lost<b> </b>in January while traveling<b> </b>between<b> </b>Minnesota<b> </b>and South Dakota, records show. U.S. Customs and Border Protection<b> </b>failed to recover it despite<b> </b>tracking down<b> </b>its last known location and<b> </b>dispatching<b> </b>officers<b> </b>there, according to the feds.</p><p>Still, data from the lost work phone was stored online and is now preserved, Reeves assured Ellis.</p><p>However, Bovino<b> </b>also<b> </b>refused<b> </b>to surrender his<b> </b>personal phone for a government review ordered<b> </b>by<b> </b>a federal judge<b> </b>in California, records show. Bovino<b> </b>apparently told officials<b> </b>it<b> </b>contained<b> </b>no<b> </b>work-related data.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" >Judge blasts Trump’s Chicago border ‘Blitz,’ extends curbs on use of force that ‘shocks the conscience’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But that’s left lawyers with few options, Illinois<b> </b>attorney<b> </b>Vikas<b> </b>Didwania told Ellis on Thursday.</p><p>“The only other way for us to access that information is to get it from the folks [Bovino] was communicating with,” Didwania said. “The people on the other side.”</p><p>Eventually, Ellis gave the Justice Department lawyers a “preview”<b> </b>of her thinking, which she said depends on “what survives”<b> </b>the pending motion to dismiss the case.</p><p>“Anyone currently employed by DHS, CBP and [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement] who was working, assigned to Operation Midway Blitz, that they will need to turn over their personal phones to be imaged,” Ellis said, “so that you can then go through and see which of them were discussing the operation with Mr. Bovino and each other.”</p><p>When warned about the litigation that might ensue, Ellis said she’d be “open to hearing about less intrusive ways to get this information.”</p><p>But, she said, she won’t let people hide behind their use of personal phones for work, “especially when there are directives, agency directives, that say they’re not to use their personal phones for work.”</p><p>“So we’ll find the least intrusive way to get this information,” Ellis said. “But we’re going to get this information.”</p>

entries.title: Trump denies disaster relief for Illinois' summer storms
entries.summary: <p>The Trump administration is denying federal disaster assistance to Illinois for aid it requested to assist in recovery efforts from severe storms throughout the summer, according to Gov. JB Pritzker’s office.</p><p>The state requested funds for individuals and the municipalities struggling with cleanup in Champaign, Cook, Ford, Fulton, McLean, Tazewell, Vermilion, and Will counties, Pritzker's office said.</p><p>Pritzker said the state would “continue to explore every available option to help our communities recover and the survivors rebuild their lives after devastating storms," including appealing the decision.</p><p>“Our communities are still picking up the pieces from the destruction caused by severe weather this summer. Donald Trump should never play politics with their homes, businesses, and infrastructure,” said Governor JB Pritzker. “When a massive storm system crosses state lines, the resulting damage should be evaluated fairly, consistently and based on the same objective standards and criteria, regardless of which state it impacts.”</p><p>Illinois has seen the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/27/200-tornadoes-illinois-2026" target="_blank" ><u>most tornadoes of any state in the nation</u></a> this year, with 212, amid a summer-long surge of severe weather.</p><p>Last month, Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/15/pritzker-extends-disaster-proclamation-to-aid-recovery-from-august-storms" target="_blank" ><u>extended</u></a> his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/18/pritzker-signs-disaster-proclamation-to-aid-recovery-after-months-of-relentless-and-unprecedented-storms" target="_blank" ><u>initial disaster proclamation</u></a> signed Aug. 18, which would have opened up temporary housing and home repair grants, low-cost loans for uninsured property damage, and “other programs to help individuals and business owners recover from the effects of this severe weather” if the request had gone through. </p><p>It included the storms in Cook County <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/27/weather-storms-heat-wind" target="_blank" ><u>July 27</u></a> that also affected DuPage, Lake, Vermillion and Will counties, in addition to storms that occurred <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/11/severe-weather-expected-in-chicago-area-and-other-areas-of-illinois" target="_blank" ><u>August 9-11</u></a>, which also made Champaign, DuPage, LaSalle, Tazewell and Will counties eligible for damage relief.</p><p>The declaration from Pritkzer came after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/30/pritzker-disaster-proclamation-tornado-flood" >another he signed</a> following severe storms in April and June.</p><p>At the time, the governor said he was confident it would be granted despite previous Trump attempts to withhold disaster funding from states that don’t politically align with him.</p><p>Last fall, a coalition of 21 attorneys general, including Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, won back nearly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/24/illinois-wins-suit-on-disaster-relief-funding-held-by-dhs-over-sanctuary-laws" target="_blank" ><u>$2 billion in disaster relief funds</u></a> Trump’s administration had attempted to withhold from states with sanctuary cities.</p><p>District Court for the District of Rhode Island Judge William E. Smith said the order was unconstitutional and violated the Administrative Procedure Act, and that the federal government had failed to consider the “public safety consequences of undermining state emergency budgets in this way.”</p><p>In a joint statement with 10 other members of Illinois’ Congressional delegation, Sen. Dick Durbin said the decision was politically motivated and “beneath the dignity of the office [Trump] holds.” </p><p>Durbin, a Democrat, said he supported Pritzker’s appeal and would “continue to do whatever I can to support Illinoisans in the aftermath of these devastating storms.”</p><p>“Much like a toddler throwing a tantrum, Donald Trump continues to punish Americans who live in states that did not support him in the last election,” Durbin said.</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks' improved play yields no reward in loss to Islanders
entries.summary: <p>If the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> turn around their season in a positive way, it's possible they look back upon their game Thursday against the Islanders as the turning point.</p><p>That sounds absurd to say after a 4-1 loss that dropped the Hawks to 1-4-0 this season, including 0-4-0 on the road.</p><p>But it was arguably the Hawks' best performance to date. It wasn't immaculate, but considering how low they set the bar on their awful opening road trip, Thursday marked noticeable improvement — even, in some ways, from their victorious home opener Tuesday.</p><p>They made quicker decisions, read plays more intelligently, completed a higher percentage of their passes, maintained work ethic and looked more cohesive as a team.</p><p>During five-on-five play, they generated 43-30 and 22-15 advantages in shot attempts and scoring chances, respectively, only to be denied by terrific Islanders goalie Ilya Sorokin from translating that onto the scoreboard.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Wyatt Kaiser sets up Cole Smith for a chance, but the puck doesn't get across the line: <a href="https://t.co/XFgQ0nI4wH">pic.twitter.com/XFgQ0nI4wH</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2108355676091359647?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 9, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Hawks' special teams weren't nearly as impressive, though, and a couple critical breakdowns — combined with bad luck — led to two Islanders goals three minutes apart that dug a deep hole halfway through the second period.</p><p>"There was a lot of stuff that I really liked about the game," coach Jeff Blashill told reporters in New York. "What I didn't like was our immaturity showed in giving up goals that we didn't have to give up.</p><p>"We need to learn how to play with that competitiveness, speed and pressure without beating ourselves."</p><p>Frank Nazar was "really going," Blashill added, even before he spoiled Sorokin's shutout bid late. A minute later, however, Nazar delivered an illegal hit to Islanders veteran Bo Horvat's head that could lead to some NHL-initiated discipline.</p><h3><b>Definitely a center</b></h3><p>The Hawks have a plethora of young forwards who they think might<i> </i>turn into centers in the NHL — or who at least have the ability to play center when needed — but they don't have many established, clear-cut centers.</p><p>That's why they called up depth center Dominic Toninato instead of winger Landon Slaggert, the last cut of training camp, to replace injured wingers Teuvo Teravainen and Andrew Mangiapane.</p><p>"[Toninato has] played a lot of center in his time in pro hockey, so he's a pretty stable guy — kind of similar to [Ryan Greene], to be honest," Blashill said Wednesday.</p><p>Toninato's presence allowed Blashill to move Oliver Moore back to wing, which is clearly where he wants Moore to be.</p><h3><b>Gauging crowds</b></h3><p>An over-capacity crowd of 20,270 unsurprisingly packed the United Center for Patrick Kane's homecoming Tuesday, and attendance should be strong again Saturday for the defending champion Hurricanes' visit.</p><p>After that, we'll get a better sense of how the Hawks' attendance this season will compare to last season, when they averaged a solid 18,949 fans per game.</p><p>Weeknight matchups against the Penguins and Jets next week will likely be two of the Hawks' least-crowded games of the season, since October is typically the toughest month to sell tickets. A number of 300-level seats, in particular, appear unsold right now.</p><p>Last year, the Hawks drew fewer than 16,650 fans to four of their six October home games — bottoming out at 15,100 — and then never again dipped below that threshold for the rest of the season.</p><p>It'll be interesting to see what exactly those Penguins and Jets attendance numbers end up being. The summer additions of Kane and Bowen Byram supposedly boosted season-ticket sales, but having eight October home games this year is a lot.</p>

entries.title: To Jerry Reinsdorf, baseball is his religion, White Sox his denomination
entries.summary: <p>If someone mentions the Chairman anywhere else in the country, Frank Sinatra is probably top of mind.</p><p>In Chicago, there’s only one Chairman — Jerry Reinsdorf.</p><p>Reinsdorf, 90, has owned the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> for more than 45 years. Do a little math, and you’ll realize that’s half his life. But for basically his entire life, Reinsdorf has been a baseball fan.</p><p>“For him, baseball is like a religion,” said Reinsdorf’s son Michael.</p><p>Michael is the president and CEO for his father’s other team, the Bulls. And though they won six NBA championships in the 1990s, Jerry desperately wanted to win a World Series. That dream finally came true in 2005.</p><p>“He’s the Bulls’ owner, but he’s not a fan like he is of baseball,” said Ozzie Guillen, who managed that team. “I think Jerry cannot live without baseball.”</p><p>It had been a mostly painful existence since then. The Sox didn’t win another postseason series until this year. And on Thursday night, they had a chance to do something the franchise hadn’t done since 1906, when they won the World Series — win a postseason series at home.</p><p>Eventually, Reinsdorf figures to hand the Sox over to minority owner Justin Ishbia, who has an option to buy the club after the 2034 season. Ishbia already is proposing plans for a new ballpark in the South Loop.</p><p>Until then, though, the Sox are Reinsdorf’s show, and he’s soaking it in.</p><p>After the Sox won Game 1 of their wild-card series in Houston last week, Reinsdorf flew down for a possible clinching celebration. When it came to fruition, he joined the team in the clubhouse and on the field for a photo.</p><p>“I said, ‘Dad, get in the picture,’ ” Michael said. “He’s like, ‘No.’ I said, ‘Get in the picture.’</p><p>“And then he’s going in the back. I’m like, ‘No.’ And then they’re all yelling, ‘Jer-ry! Jer-ry!’ It was a surreal moment.”</p><p>It was a reward for seeing through an organizational rebuild that was long overdue.</p><p>“Just taking a look at his face as this team rolls along and stays relevant is something that is pretty gratifying just for me,” said Steve Stone, the Sox’ longtime TV analyst and a close friend of Reinsdorf’s.</p><p>Stone has known Reinsdorf since his playing career ended after the 1981 season. Reinsdorf wanted Stone, who pitched for the Sox in 1973 and 1977-78, to be a coach on the team he had just bought from Bill Veeck. Stone wanted to see where his TV gig would take him. But they became friends.</p><p>“Long before the Sox existed in the world of Jerry Reinsdorf, he loved baseball,” Stone said.</p><p>Reinsdorf grew up in Brooklyn and was a devoted Dodgers fan. He attended Jackie Robinson’s first game at Ebbets Field. His favorite player was Hall of Famer Pee Wee Reese.</p><p>“He told me a story that, once he got in baseball, he got on an elevator with Pee-Wee Reese, and he was tongue-tied,” Michael said. “He couldn’t even speak. As a kid, that’s who he looked up to. That was everything to him.”</p><p>As an adult, the Sox have been everything to him. Think about all the leadership changes of other teams in town, even within families. Reinsdorf has been a constant with the Sox — for better or, in the view of many fans, worse.</p><p>“I believe Jerry is one of the more misunderstood public men in our city,” Stone said. “People think he doesn’t want to win.”</p><p>“The last few years were really difficult for him,” Michael said of the three consecutive seasons with more than 100 losses. “He’s a passionate baseball guy, and he really wanted to turn it around. That was really important to him.”</p><p>Guillen visited Reinsdorf in his Rate Field suite Wednesday and congratulated him for the Sox’ season. He also expressed how happy he was that Reinsdorf was able to see it and that he was part of it.</p><p>“When he was in the [2005] World Series, he never was really around the team,” Guillen said. “Now I see him on the field enjoying this moment, because he never thought the kids could do what they’re doing right now.”</p><p>In fact, Guillen thinks this team has surpassed his championship team on Reinsdorf’s list of favorites.</p><p>“He’s got a very soft spot for the 1983 ballclub,” Guillen said of the division champs. “That’s his life. I don’t know why.</p><p>“If you put them on a scale, ’83, 2026 and 2005.”</p><p>“Later in life, we have a tendency to appreciate things more,” Stone said. “And he’s getting a great deal of enjoyment, tremendous amount of satisfaction. He’s ecstatic about this Sox team. It’s very important to him.”</p>

entries.title: White Sox focused on ALDS, not most recent CBA proposal
entries.summary: <p>With the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1, and Major League Baseball team owners universally expected to lockout the players–just as they did on Dec. 1, 2021–when it does, MLB released a new proposal on Thursday as part of their ongoing negotiations with the players’ association (MLBPA).</p><p>As it turns out, the hours before Game of the American League Division Series, with the White Sox hoping to clinch a postseason series victory in front of their home fans for the first time in 120 years, are not the perfect time to get thoughtful answers about the future of labor relations for the sport.</p><p>“I haven't had time to think about it,” said Sox outfielder <b>Tristan Peters</b>. “I haven't really formulated an opinion yet.”</p><p>“Respectfully, I could not care less in this moment right now,” said manager <b>Will Venable</b>.</p><p>Notable details include shortening the regular season to 154 games, expanding the ALDS to a best-of-seven, allowing higher seeds to pick their playoff opponents, and making Monday a standard off day across the league with the exception of some limited nationally broadcasted matchups.</p><p>In their response, the MLBPA seized upon a different, less-publicized element of the proposal.</p><p>“Unfortunately, the league once again made clear that all of its proposals are contingent on the players’ agreement to a salary cap,” the MLBPA’s statement read in part. “[A salary cap is] a system that guts player rights and compensation.”</p><p>A salary cap has long been, and clearly appears to still be a non-starter for the MLBPA. As such, pontificating on the impacts of league-proposed changes to the structure of the sport that include a salary cap is more of an exercise for the public than something with which the players are going to engage.</p><p>Or at least, that is what can be gleaned by two separate MLBPA team representatives on the White Sox roster respectfully declining comment on the proposal to the Sun-Times.</p><h3><b>You know it when you feel it</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Asked about his young roster potentially getting overhyped before playing Game 3 in front of the most intense and packed crowd of their lives, Venable seemed unconcerned.</p><p>“I hadn't thought about that,” Venable said. “We're not going to put any governors on that or want to do anything but embrace the excitement and embrace the energy.”</p><p>But after his team struck out 19 times, an MLB postseason record in a nine-inning game, and chased out of the zone at stratospheric levels against Guardians pitchers <b>Foster Griffin</b>, <b>Tim Herrin</b>, <b>Cade Smith</b> and others, Venable felt the need to address it.</p><p>“I'm not sure that there was anything that myself or [hitting coach <b>Derek Shomon]</b> or anybody else could have said to prepare them for that,” Venable said. “They had to experience it for themselves. So we have that experience in our back pocket now, and we'll talk about it with the guys.”</p><h3><b>Twilight games?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The White Sox got to host a proper nighttime ‘blackout game’ for Thursday’s ALDS Game 4. If and when they advance to face the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALCS, the first two games at Tropicana Field will be in primetime at 7:00pm CT.</p><p>For Games 3 and 4 at Rate Field, the start times will be 5:00pm CT. It’ll be a blackout game by the time <b>Grant Taylor</b> is pitching, at least.</p>

entries.title: Unimpressed with Sky coach Tyler Marsh? Let's talk about it
entries.summary: <p>I imagined the collective groan, the dissatisfied emojis in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> fan group chats at last week’s news that coach Tyler Marsh is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/10/01/sky-to-bring-back-coach-tyler-marsh-for-third-season" >coming back</a> for a third season.</p><p>Marsh has been a tough sell for Sky fans still wounded by the abrupt firing of Teresa Weatherspoon in 2024 and now thoroughly unimpressed by the two losing seasons that followed.</p><p>Why does Marsh get such a long leash when the patience for Weatherspoon, a Hall of Fame player, was so thin?</p><p>To temper some of this angst: Marsh’s return in 2027 does not mean the Sky have decided he is the coach of the future.</p><p>There was considerable disagreement, according to multiple sources, about whether to keep him. In his exit interview, general manager Jeff Pagliocca said Marsh’s youth, combined with all the injuries, meant it would be unfair to give him the boot. Taken as a whole, his comments sounded more like punting the decision to next year than committing long-term.</p><p>So I’ll keep front and center the question that I've thought about most this past year: Is Marsh a good enough coach for this team?</p><p>I should know by now, right? After watching 88 games over the last two years, attending dozens of practices and straining to listen to his huddle speeches, I should be able to tell how good he is.</p><p>But I can't. And I think that’s OK.</p><p>I do feel confident that he has the potential to be a strong leader in this league.</p><p>He’s trusted by two of the best coaches, Becky Hammon and Natalie Nakase, which speaks volumes. He’s committed to the collective struggle and purpose of the WNBA. He’s humble in the truest sense of the word.</p><p>If you’ve heard these points already, it’s because I think Sky fans, many of whom have followed the league since the beginning, will appreciate them. So I slip them in here and there, trying to interrupt their certainty that <i>he just ain’t got it</i>.</p><p>It usually works for a moment. I’ll see appreciation, a softening flicker across their faces. But it subsides the moment the team loses another game. His hesitation to call timeouts during opposing runs. The team’s inability to close games. Then the fury, the indignation, returns.</p><p>And I get it. Sports give us a release for big emotions, sweeping conclusions. They offer the satisfaction of issuing collective judgments. This coach is good. This one is bad. This player is underrated. This one is a flop.</p><p>Plus, this is Chicago: We want a winner, not just a good guy.</p><p>I just think we should acknowledge how hard it is to know whether someone is a winner <i>before</i> they’ve, you know, done the winning.</p><p>What about when they’re still developing? When they’re in a muddled situation?</p><p>With Marsh, I get that his reputation and fit for the WNBA aren’t enough to establish his potential as a head coach. He could be a great leader of women who’s still better suited to being an assistant.</p><p>I do think he’s got some head coaching chops. He’s a talented designer of plays, especially for young center Kamilla Cardoso. I like his offensive system, based on ball movement and pace. I like that his players give him props for being transparent and collaborative.</p><p>On the flip side, I think he needs to be bolder, more willing to put his stamp on a given game, on the organization, on the locker room. What exactly are his players learning from him? How is he molding them? I see those answers more clearly from Hammon, Nakase and Cheryl Reeve.</p><p>Where I’m most hung up, though, is on the fit for this particular organization. Sometimes I think he might be a better fit for the Storm, Sun or even the Mystics, where development is the priority. He loves to talk about how growth isn’t linear, how his young players deserve grace and patience.</p><p>But the Sky’s defining characteristic at this point is their rejection of the concept of a multiyear rebuild. The team is expected to finish in the top half of the standings every year, but without the runway franchises often give themselves to accumulate draft assets and develop young players.</p><p>That’s a tough needle for anyone to thread.</p>

entries.title: Students, faculty and neighbors press DePaul University to reopen its art museum
entries.summary:
T.J. Brescia, a 19-year-old DePaul University sophomore, convinced three of his friends to attend a silent demonstration on the Lincoln Park campus Thursday.

He was among more than 130 students, faculty, staff, arts leaders and Lincoln Park neighbors who lined up from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m. just outside the DePaul Art Museum, 935 W. Fullerton Ave., to send a message to university leadership: They want the museum, which closed on June 30, to reopen.

The art museum ceased operations “to ensure long-term financial sustainability for our university,” university leadership said in a statement. Days after the initial announcement, university staff, faculty, students, alumni and notable Chicago arts leaders added their names to a letter of opposition to the closure. As of publication time, the letter has nearly 4,000 signatures.

“This has justifiably p - - - - - everyone I know off,” said Brescia’s friend, DePaul sophomore Theo Tran, 20.

Brescia said he never got to visit the museum, but as an art lover, he is disappointed. “I'm here today because I would love to eventually see it reopen,” he said.

Campus security was not present, but nearly a dozen uniformed police officers kept watch from underneath the nearby CTA tracks. A few school administrators were also keeping an eye on things.

The demonstration was organized anonymously, as word circulated online with the hashtag “#waitingatDPAM.” A flyer described the event as “an open call to the public to gather in line at the closed doors” of the museum.

Though closed to the public, it still holds the majority of the university’s collection of more than 4,000 objects.

“It is strange to be in a building where two of the floors are kind of remnants of the past,” said Laura-Caroline de Lara, the museum’s director and only full-time employee. She has served as director since January 2022.

“The galleries are empty. The lights are turned off,” de Lara said. “It's strange for a place that had been so lively and warm.”

But the museum is receiving plenty of loan requests, de Lara said. “I think it's been one of the largest years on record for other institutions requesting works from us, which is incredible, and means that the collection still has a life,” she said.

De Lara said she’s even working on several multi-year loan agreements for specific artworks. And plenty of DePaul professors still use the museum’s collections for their syllabi, especially the museum studies department.

Though she had no hand in organizing the demonstration, de Lara attended with her family. “My charge is still caring for an incredible collection, and for ensuring that that incredible collection gets some play outside of storage,” she said.

Cynthia Noble, executive director of Art on the Mart, also attended the protest.

“I want to support the students and the faculty here at a Catholic college because I am a Catholic,” Noble said. “Pope [Leo XIV] actually just came out and said incredible things about the importance of human creation versus AI creation. I think there's a great irony to a Catholic university closing down its visual arts museum at this time.”

DePaul issued a statement to the Sun-Times and WBEZ Thursday, saying the university “welcomes this peaceful demonstration in support of the arts in Chicago. The decision to stop operations at the DePaul Art Museum was a difficult one, as many institutions around the country are facing budgetary constraints.”

The statement confirmed DePaul still has zero plans to sell the art collection or building. A task force including several faculty members has been formed, and it's working closely with the university’s president and provost to reimagine the future of the art museum and its collections.

The museum was considered an important local venue for underrepresented artists. Its collection also includes photography by artists including Andy Warhol and Chicagoans Dawoud Bey and Paul D’Amato. The museum also boasts a significant collection of West African objects and Latino art.

“All of us want to see DPAM open again as soon as possible,” said Brother Mark Elder, a muralist and art professor. He was the first person in line Thursday.

Members of the art museum task force, which includes faculty members such as Elder and Mark DeLancey, an art history professor, said they’ve been meeting nearly every week.

“This is a question about what we want the character of this museum to be going forward,” DeLancey said. The task force is scheduled to present a report at a faculty council meeting Dec. 2, he said.

“We're not out to protest anything beyond the closure of the DePaul Art Museum,” DeLancey said. “We hope that the image of people lining up before doors that are closed to them will make the point.”

entries.title: White Sox fans, does it get any better than this? Just saying — it might not
entries.summary: <p>As the start of Game 4 of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a>’ American League Division Series against the Guardians neared Thursday at Rate Field, one had to wonder:</p><p>Does it get any better than this?</p><p>No, really, though, does it?</p><p>Because even for the young, ascendant Sox, it might not. Come to think of it, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/07/white-sox-guardians-mlb-postseason-rate-field-south-side-jose-ramirez-miguel-vargas" target="_blank" >especially for the Sox, it might not</a>.</p><p>Something that has gotten lost in the Sox’ sudden, startling success this season is just how fragile the whole thing was from the beginning. The Sox played in what was, undeniably, a bad division. They played in the lesser of the two leagues, the balance of power as off as ever. They got the Astros, the worst full-season division champion by record in major league history, in the wild-card round and the Guardians, the lowest-spending team in the AL, after that. Suffice it to say, the Sox, as surprisingly good as they were, didn’t need any miracles to reach this point.</p><p>And by the way, fragile can still be quite beautiful. A 40,000-strong “Blackout” on the South Side in October, with all the excitement, hope and catharsis therein, more than qualifies.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">A veritable blackout at the Rate. <br>And they’re playing the awesome “Pirates of the Caribbean” hype video! <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/WhiteSox?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#WhiteSox</a> <a href="https://t.co/GiqCs6Pkaw">pic.twitter.com/GiqCs6Pkaw</a></p>— Jeff Agrest #🟦 (@JeffAgrest) <a href="https://x.com/JeffAgrest/status/2108348108597768601?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 9, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>But a dangerous uncertainty loomed for the Sox in more ways than one.</p><p>First, getting past the Guardians — no easy feat — would necessitate taking a giant step up in weight class for an AL Championship Series against the 98-win Rays, who swept the Yankees in the divisional round. One way to look at the Rays is that they’re everything the Sox aspire to be: a high-achieving, thoroughly professional outfit with no significant weaknesses aside from an inclination to spend modestly. Offensively, the Rays are the cream of the AL crop at getting on base, hitting for average and not striking out. Their starting pitching allowed the fewest walks and hits per inning in the AL. Beat this team in a best-of-seven? The Sox might need luck just to steal a game or two.</p><p>But the very real threat of a bitterly contentious MLB lockout hovers over the 2027 season, a critical one for the Sox if they are to build on this momentum. There also are questions relating to future ownership arrangements and stadium possibilities, though these factors seemingly aren’t as pressing.</p><p>And then there’s the simple, nagging possibility the Sox won’t be better next year or that their “better” won’t be good enough to carry them this far.</p><p>It’s a movie Sox fans have seen before.</p><p>Go back to October of 2021. The young, talented Sox had ripped off 93 wins for their first winning record in a full season since 2012. Even after they lost to the Astros in a four-game ALDS, hopes were high for a continued ascent.</p><p>“We’re going to keep growing,” Gavin Sheets said after homering for the Sox’ only run of Game 4 at the Rate.</p><p>“We have more work to do,” manager Tony La Russa promised.</p><p>Cue an 81-81 clunker that ran the train right off the rails.</p><p>The 2008 Sox fought through injuries in an 89-win roller coaster ride in 2008 and they, too, made it as far as Game 4 of the divisional round before being eliminated by the Rays at what was then called U.S. Cellular Field.</p><p>“Am I satisfied? No,” manager Ozzie Guillen said. “I want to be in it longer [next year].”</p><p>Then came a 2009 tumble to below .500.</p><p>The 2005 world champion Sox missed the playoffs the following year, and by 2007 the record was 72-90.</p><p>Ninety-five wins in 2000 became a mere 83 in 2001.</p><p>Everyone who watched the early-1990s Sox rise still can taste the bitterness of the 1994 labor stoppage that killed the season, taking a prime Sox World Series shot with it.</p><p>And maybe the best example of all: the breakthrough Sox of 1983, who won 99 games and brought postseason baseball to the South Side for the first time since 1959, only to ride off the cliff at 74-88 in 1984. At the All-Star break in ’84, the Sox actually led the AL West. From there, it was nothing but momentum-killing, goodwill-killing disaster.</p><p>You just don’t know what’s going to happen, as current Sox manager Will Venable explained to the Sun-Times last month, citing his time as associate manager of the Rangers in 2023, when they won it all, and in 2024, when they were just another losing team.</p><p>“I don’t think that we can make the assumption that this is going to exist next year,” Venable told beat writer James Fegan. “I’m hopeful because it’s going to be a lot of the same guys, but DNA changes. I saw it in Texas. Got this amazing group of guys, win a World Series, have success. Offseason maybe looks a little different. Guys are in different situations, whatever. Personal stuff happens. Next year, you’re trying to create the magic, and it’s hard to do.”</p><p>So enjoy this Sox ride, come what may.</p><p>Does it get any better?</p><p>One does have to wonder.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/07/white-sox-guardians-mlb-postseason-rate-field-south-side-jose-ramirez-miguel-vargas" target="_blank" >Will White Sox ever win a postseason series in Chicago? entries.title: White Sox have overachieved to contend this early, but taking next step will require more pitching depth
entries.summary: <p>Even without being able to poll the front office representatives from all 30 MLB teams that weigh in on the award, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> general manager Chris Getz is getting some Executive of the Year votes; probably a lot of them.</p><p>That’s how things go when a team projected to finish in last place is still standing in the second week in October, after sending three players to the All-Star Game. But also, inarguably, Getz and his front office have brought in a lot of players who have overperformed expectations, and proven to be — or been developed into — far more valuable contributors than the public and industry believed when they were acquired.</p><p>“Chris is just a talented leader,” said special assistant David Keller, who keyed international pursuits of Munetaka Murakami and Anthony Kay. “He first and foremost did a tremendous job of identifying people who are great teammates.”</p><p>Murakami, Miguel Vargas, Chase Meidroth, Tristan Peters, Sean Newcomb, Randal Grichuk–even low-cost free-agent signing Erick Fedde was hearing his name chanted in unison by the home crowd during Game 4 of the American League Division Series.</p><p>If everyone knew when Getz was hired that by the end of his third full season, the most pressing question was whether he built a roster that could seriously compete for the AL pennant, the tenor of his introductory press conference would have been a little different.</p><p>“He’s done a terrific job and I really appreciate all the times you guys have written about you were wrong when I hired Chris,” White Sox chairman Jerry Reinsdorf quipped after his team swept the Astros out of the wild-card series.</p><p>That said, the question of whether Getz can build a championship-level roster is now the one at hand. It’s a great problem to have, but it is now a pressing one.</p><p>“As you move higher, the jumps get harder to make,” assistant general manager Josh Barfield told the Sun-Times. “You have to be sharp. We also don't have the bullets [to trade] that we had when we first got here.”</p><p>At present, the shortage of bullets reveals itself in the form of neither of the two pitchers the White Sox acquired at the trade deadline–Luis Castillo and Huascar Brazoban–cracking their ALDS roster, as they held fast onto top prospects like Caleb Bonemer and Billy Carlson in discussions with other teams.</p><p>And the perceptible gap between the Sox and the contenders they suddenly find themselves going toe-to-toe with, is pitching depth. Other teams have narrow playoff rotations, the South Siders have Sean Burke and a series of bullpen games, where ace reliever Grant Taylor is competing for the team lead in postseason innings pitched, and getting knocked around in Game 4 of a series where he’s already logged 5 ⅓ innings.</p><p>“I've been asked many times on eventually is this going to catch up with us,” said Getz before Game 3. “At least in the 2026 season, you look at the schedule, and well, it's worked for us. Why can't it further? We can find plenty of reasons why it may not. Eventually, you just run out. But these guys really take care of themselves.”</p><p>As Getz has intimated more than once, the Sox are playing with house money this season. Every step a seemingly unsustainable stretching of limited pitching resources gets them is another step farther than any reasonable person would have had them going. The question for a White Sox team that wants to win best-of-seven series now and in the future is not their unorthodox use of the playoff-worthy arms they have, but having more playoff-worthy arms.</p><p>Building a playoff team out of undervalued journeyman pitchers only holds its charm for so long. The reward of a stunning season where the Sox performed beyond their wildest dreams is a mandate to improve upon it, and the best teams in the league laying your shortcomings bare on a national stage.</p>

entries.title: White Sox headed to Cleveland for Game 5 after Grant Taylor, pitching staff routed in 9-5 loss
entries.summary: <p>This week was supposed to bring the White Sox clinching a postseason series win at home for the first time in 120 years.</p><p>“It sucks, you want to do that for the fans,” said second baseman Chase Meidroth after his club’s 9-5 loss to the Guardians in Game 4 of the American League Division Series. “We all wanted it so bad for the fans.”</p><p>But behind 18 runs and 17 walks allowed in two games to a Guardians offense that finished 11th in the AL in runs scored, but upgraded at the trade deadline in a way the Sox pitching staff was not, it won’t be happening. Not in this series, and without an about-face in two days, not this year at all.</p><p>“Certainly, that's something that we wanted to give our fans,” said manager Will Venable. “I think we just want to win this series however possible, and wherever that is, we'll take it.”</p><p>It’s fitting that an inter-division battle between Chicago and Cleveland, separated by a game in head-to-head matchups, separated by a game in the AL Central standings, is heading to a final showdown at Progressive Field. At least that’s how a quiet Sox clubhouse is rationalizing two deflating and lopsided losses in front of sold-out crowds.</p><p>“I got asked that yesterday and said we turned the page today,” said outfielder Sam Antonacci, asked about turning the page. “We turned the page, but we lost. So, we’ll turn three pages and hopefully win.”</p><p>Staff ace Sean Burke walked to the bullpen after the fifth, when the Sox held a brief 4-3 lead and it seemed like he might get the final outs, if Grant Taylor could hold the Guardians at bay. Instead he’ll be available for Game 5; a reason for confidence against a Cleveland team that needed a sixth inning to even register a hit against him in Game 2.</p><p>But Taylor did not hold the Guardians at bay, instead allowing all six hitters he faced to reach in a six-run sixth that assured a return to Progressive Field on Saturday. Anthony Kay had begun the inning and retired one of the three hitters he faced. Before him, stalwart rookie Hagen Smith walked the bases loaded and could not complete the first.</p><p>“Body felt good, stuff felt good, just didn’t execute,” said Taylor, downplaying workload concerns. “It truly was just execution. I walked two guys and they put the ball in play.”</p><p>With Burke at the ready, it’s hard to argue that the White Sox are fully out of pitching, or out of hope for knocking off an 85-win Cleveland team that has taxed their own staff, and asked presumptive Game 5 starter Gavin Williams to get the last three outs of Game 4. But it’s hard to figure what would look different if a Sox postseason pitching plan built on bullpen games was running out of gas.</p><p>Erick Fedde had the performances of a lifetime on Thursday, rescuing Smith from his first-inning jam, and keeping the Guardians scoreless until the fifth. A sold-out crowd dressed in black chanted his name in a way the 33-year-old former first-round pick had never previously enjoyed.</p><p>“Probably the most surreal moment of my career,” Fedde said. “Hard to put into words.”</p><p>Yet when Fedde departed with one out in the fifth, there was still more than half the game to go and not enough Sox arms to navigate it. There were also no answers left for third baseman Jose Ramirez, who looks rejuvenated after homering and driving in three to send the series back to Cleveland.</p><p>“Every guy will have their jersey on in the bullpen ready to throw [in Game 5], whether they feel good, whether they feel bad.” Fedde said. “I believe in these guys.”</p><p>Inspiring, but also a realistic view of what Sox pitching will be working from at the end of a series that’s stretched them to their limits.</p>

entries.title: DeKalb woman charged in 2023 Austin shooting
entries.summary: <p>A DeKalb woman is facing attempted murder charges for a May 2023 shooting in Austin, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Amya Vanwinkle, 23, is facing a count of first-degree attempted murder, police said. She was arrested in DeKalb Wednesday.</p><p>Vanwinkle is accused of shooting an unidentified 43-year-old in the back in the 4900 block of West Ohio Street on May 16, 2023, at 1 a.m., police said. The victim was taken to Stroger Hospital in serious condition.</p><p>Vanwinkle is due in court Friday.</p>

entries.title: Woman fatally stabbed during argument in Chicago Lawn
entries.summary: <p>Charges are pending for a person who stabbed a woman in the chest with a sharp object, killing her during an argument Thursday night in the Chicago Lawn neighborhood on the Southwest Side. </p><p>The woman, 48, was arguing with a person she knew around 10:10 p.m. in the 3400 block of West 59th Place when he pulled out a sharp object and stabbed her, Chicago police said. </p><p>She was stabbed in the chest and was taken to Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn, where was pronounced dead, police said. Her name has not been released. </p><p>The male fled the scene and was found by officers in the 3400 block of West 59th Place. Officers found the weapon and placed him in custody. </p><p>Charges were pending. </p>

entries.title: Trump: the 'Picasso' of corruption
entries.summary: <p>Trayon White, a member of the city council in the District of Columbia, just walked away from a hung jury in a bribery trial. The facts were kind of wild. Though White admitted to accepting $35,000 in cash from a city contractor (who turned out to be an FBI informant), and the prosecution presented evidence that he tucked white envelopes full of bills totaling between $5,000 and $15,000 into his jacket pocket on several occasions, the jury was deadlocked. Whatever. Juries are unpredictable. The point is, this run-of-the-mill public corruption case got prosecuted in a D.C. courtroom when, just a few blocks away, the president of the United States is accepting bribes and favors that dwarf anything White could even dream of.</p><p>Journalists love expressions like "the most corrupt since Watergate" or the "worst official corruption since Teapot Dome." </p><p>The trouble with those formulations is that they suggest that Watergate and Teapot Dome are the standards against which wrongdoing should be judged. If what we're seeing now is only the "worst since," then it means it isn't quite to that level. The truth is that nothing — no scandal, no graft in American history — comes remotely close to the level of corruption the Trump administration is perpetrating.</p><p>Every single day brings news of some flagrant conflict of interest, bribe, emolument, kickback, fraud or theft. Most of it involves Donald Trump himself and his family. But just as a fish rots from the head, Trump's example has contaminated his administration. A glance at this week's papers reveals that former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, before she left office, finalized a government purchase of several aging Boeing jets from one of her campaign donors, paying way above market value. There's another ongoing probe of a Noem hire who was reportedly paid $19,000 a week.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-600000" name="module-600000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>When she wasn't busy slandering Renee Good as a "domestic terrorist" or posing in front of men locked up in El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center, or CECOT, megaprison, Noem was reportedly awarding no-bid contracts to cronies for a $220 million ad campaign that featured her on horseback at Mount Rushmore, among other things. Contracts totaling $143 million were allegedly given to an entity that was incorporated only 11 days before the solicitation.</p><p>The role of Corey Lewandowski seems totally on the up and up: He was, in effect, Noem's deputy, yet took no salary for nearly two years' work during a time when he was widely believed to be her romantic partner. A number of executives complained to the White House that they were being asked to funnel funds to Lewandowski's entities.</p><p>Everywhere you look, the pay-for-play nature of this government surfaces like herpes. The Campaign Legal Center keeps a running roster of donors who've received valuable posts, pardons, tariff waivers, regulatory relief or contracts from the White House. It runs to more than 40 pages of small print.</p><p>Nothing is untainted. Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding party in the Bahamas? You might suppose that the Trump family, after extracting $2.7 billion in wealth since the paterfamilias's reelection in 2024, could afford the weekend party at a private island. But no, it was bankrolled by a Russian oligarch with close ties to Vladimir Putin. The bride, Bettina Trump, was offended that small-minded people might object, explaining that Umar Kremlev is a "dear friend" who hosted the party as a gift "for which we were and remain incredibly grateful." As Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, put it: "A toaster is a wedding gift. A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else."</p><p>If someone, even a "dear friend," shells out several hundred thousand dollars to celebrate your wedding, is there any doubt in anyone's mind that he will want something in return? Is there any doubt that this is not a gift, but a bribe or a "stay sold" measure? Of course not. But beyond that, imagine being fine with accepting such gifts indirectly from a war criminal. Apples/trees. (Trump Jr. has since said he will reimburse Kremlev.)</p><p>Nothing the Trump administration does can be taken at face value. Just as judges can no longer expect Department of Justice lawyers to be telling the truth and acting in good faith (the "presumption of regularity" is moribund), citizens can no longer take it for granted that the government is acting in the public interest and not aiming to line the pockets of the Trump family and friends. Let's take three examples: kidnapping Nicolas Maduro and trying him, pursuing an aggressive deportation regime, and negotiating to end the war in Ukraine.</p><p>The Maduro capture, which convinced Trump that he could easily topple the Iranian regime the following month, was in no sense an effort to improve the lives of the Venezuelan people. It was plunder. Recall that Trump's criticism of Operation Iraqi Freedom was that we failed to "take the oil." No surprise, then, that taking Venezuela's oil was foremost on his mind after the Maduro snatch-and-grab. </p><p>Trump's White House boasts that "In the biggest oil deal in world history, Trump has secured U.S. majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves in Venezuela." Some of Trump's personal and political allies are swooping in to take advantage of the Venezuela opportunities. Meanwhile, the funds from the sale of this oil have supposedly been moved to an account in Qatar, but the administration has not shared a detailed breakdown of these funds with Congress or the public. Trump has claimed that the oil windfall has paid for the Venezuelan military operation "many, many, many times over" but there has been zero transparency about how much oil has been sold, where the proceeds are and how they've been spent.</p><p>Doubtless the Trump administration is sincere in its demonization of immigrants and indifference to the suffering of those it wrongly rounds up, detains and deports (sometimes to third countries with which the immigrants have no ties, including countries with appalling human rights records). But if there's also a way to pay off big donors while enjoying all this human suffering and injustice, all the better. The GEO Group and CoreCivic, two firms that operate private prisons and detention centers, donated $2.8 million to Trump's reelection effort and inauguration. Since then, GEO has been awarded more than $1 billion in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement contracts. CoreCivic sold two facilities to ICE for $1.5 billion. Perhaps it was a coincidence. "So, $1.5 billion just for the facilities," former senior ICE official remarked to CalMatters. "And how many migrants are ever going to come in and out of there who are national security and public safety threats? The people that we actually do need to keep off the streets."</p><p>Remember the attempted shakedown of Volodymyr Zelensky in 2025, when Trump and Vice President JD Vance teamed up to bully him in the Oval Office and Trump demanded access to Ukraine's rare-earth minerals? That spirit persists. According to New York Times reporting this week, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who are notionally negotiating to end the Russia/Ukraine war, have "expanded" their talks to include a multibillion-dollar oil deal that would benefit "Middle Eastern business executives with ties to" — guess who? Kushner and Witkoff.</p><p>While "there is no indication that Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff themselves stand to profit," the Times writes with considerable understatement that it is "a striking intermingling of personal business ties with geopolitics."</p><h3>Tainted transactions </h3><p>The Trump sons are doing well, too. Companies in which Eric and Donald Jr. have invested have been awarded $3.2 billion in direct government business and secured another $3.1 billion in future contract options, according to a Washington Post analysis.</p><p>The list of corrupt, tainted transactions is virtually endless. On April 30, the tobacco company Reynolds American donated $5 million through a subsidiary to MAGA Inc. Executives were then invited to lunch at one of Trump's clubs. They complained about an Food and Drug Administration regulation of vaping cigarettes. Trump made a call then and there to Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and, voila, the regulation was changed a few days later.</p><p>Other than the Trump memecoin, the most direct pathway for dollars to Trump's pocket has been the scheme to sell early access to Truth Social posts. For $100,000 a month, Trump will sell you his often market-relevant posts a few seconds before everyone else sees them. The funds would go directly to Trump Media, which Trump owns. Attempting to defend this corrupt arrangement in a federal court on Wednesday, a Department of Justice lawyer compared it to Franklin Roosevelt's "fireside chats." The judge immediately interrupted him: "Well, President Roosevelt didn't charge money for his fireside chats, did he?"</p><p>As Brendan Ballou, the lawyer representing media organizations who are suing to stop Trump's Truth Social grift, put it, "In some ways, Trump is the Picasso of corruption. He comes up with schemes that just wouldn't occur to you or I, and the Truth Social one is an example of that."</p><p>The MAGA intellectuals — and yes, there are some — imagine that they are keeping the U.S. from decline by supporting Trump. They say things like "Import the Third World, become the Third World." But it is Trump's record-shattering corruption that is rushing us toward Third World status. Trayon White at least faced a jury. Trump's only reckoning can come from the ballot box, and while that may be encouraging, it's not nearly proportional to the destruction he is wreaking.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of the Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d20000" name="module-d20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Misunderstanding leads to birthday blues
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a man in my late 60s who hasn't had a family birthday party since I was a child. My mother's birthday is seven days from mine, so celebrations were always for her, and mine were sort of lost in the shuffle. This was never a problem for me when I was younger, but as I get older, I think it would be nice to have a party.</p><p>When I was 50, there was a surprise party for me, but shortly after the party started, I was informed that I was sharing the event with Mom. When we sat down together to open gifts, Mom had many, and I had few. Later, many guests apologized and said they had not been told the party was for me, just Mom.</p><p>I may have appeared upset, but, because I did not want to hurt her feelings, I told my sister I was uncomfortable being celebrated. She spread this to other family members, which is the reason everyone has avoided celebrations for me ever since. Is this fixable without hurting anyone, or has this misunderstanding doomed me to a partyless life? — <i>NOT A PARTY ANIMAL</i></p><p><b>DEAR NOT A PARTY ANIMAL:</b> You are not "doomed." You just need to start taking responsibility for your own parties. For the next few years, organize your birthday gatherings exactly the way you want them to be. Be clear in your invitation that the party is for you only. (Also make sure someone plans a separate soiree for Mom.) This will show others you are open to celebrating yourself. It will also let them know how you like your parties in case they decide to surprise you again in the future.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I live in an apartment complex for low-income elderly or disabled people. It's not assisted living; if we need help, we must hire whatever help isn't covered by insurance.</p><p>The 94-year-old man next door has become 100% bedridden and has requested to go to a nursing home. He is also very hard of hearing and completely immobile. The woman who cares for him (and also has power of attorney) does a good job when she's there, but she is social and is consistently late because she stops outdoors and talks to other residents before coming in to tend to him. Today she drove in at 8:30 a.m. but didn't come inside until after 9, meaning he'd been left for more than 18 hours between meals and changing.</p><p>Often he calls out for help, but at 85, I cannot and should not try to help him. It's upsetting. Is there something I can do? Should I just mind my own business? — <i>FRUSTRATED NEIGHBOR</i></p><p><b>DEAR NEIGHBOR:</b> It's understandable that you're upset. This man needs to be moved to a nursing home immediately if not sooner. Have you spoken to the caregiver? She'll need to coordinate between his insurance company, the state or local department of senior services, and possibly Medicaid. If you're feeling generous, offer to help her research what's needed to get him into a safer environment.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</p>

entries.title: Trump's obsessions may help bury GOP chances in Maine and elsewhere
entries.summary: <p>Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, is facing one of the toughest reelection battles of her lifetime. And <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6132984-maine-senate-debate-collins-jackson/" target="_blank" >at Tuesday night’s debate</a>, she was clearly on the defensive.</p><p>This race should not have been this competitive. Collins has held this seat for five terms. And while Maine has voted for the Democrat in every presidential election since 1992, it still has a fierce independent streak and a healthy Republican base.</p><p>But this year is different. President Donald Trump’s approval numbers are abysmal, his tariffs and his war in Iran have tanked our economy, and he seems focused on things that would actively turn voters off — like spending taxpayer dollars on propaganda ads, vanity construction projects, fighting with journalists and punishing his enemies.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a10000" name="module-a10000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>And all the while, he’s telling voters that their affordability concerns are a hoax. It’s hard to run on two more years of … this.</p><p>In Maine, Trump’s trade war with bordering Canada is a particular pain point, evidenced by how badly Collins tried to distance herself from the tariffs during the debate.</p><p>She boasted that she fought to keep a few important items off Trump’s tariff list, including concrete, pulp and road salt.</p><p>Her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, a longtime Maine legislator, delivered a response that should become a mantra for every Dem running this cycle: “<a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/06/politics/maine-senate-debate-susan-collins-troy-jackson-takeaways" target="_blank" >We can’t eat road salt.</a>”</p><p>It was a simple and straightforward acknowledgment that most Americans are struggling to pay their bills, put gas in their cars, put food on the table, and meanwhile Trump’s tariffs are making all of that harder. Collins saving the road salt doesn’t help with any of it.</p><p>But it’s more than road salt.</p><p>So much of what Trump and Republicans are offering in this eleventh-hour desperation won’t solve Americans’ affordability crisis either.</p><p>Trump’s obsession with building monuments to himself won’t help a farmer in Iowa put diesel in his tractor. We can’t eat ballrooms.</p><p>Trump’s <a class="Link" href="https://nymag.com/intelligencer/article/trumps-ai-republicans-impossible-place.html" target="_blank" >cheerleading for artificial intelligence</a> while the rest of the world panics about the power-hungry tech bros leading the charge won’t put money in the pocket of a single mom working three jobs in Trenton, New Jersey. We can’t eat data centers.</p><p>Trump’s endless war and its global economic destruction isn’t helping the North Carolina apple farmer who lost it all in Hurricane Helene. We can’t eat Iran strikes.</p><p>Trump’s fixation with punishing political enemies, and Republican lawmakers’ preening efforts to oblige him in Congress won’t help the laid-off autoworker in Pontiac, Michigan. We can’t eat Jack Smith hearings.</p><p>Trump’s constant grifting, self-dealing and his family’s efforts to line their own pockets through crypto and billion-dollar Pentagon contracts aren’t helping the family in Ames, Iowa, struggling to pay their cancer treatment bills. We can’t eat corruption.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/05/media/politico-white-house-print-pool-media-cnn-msnow" target="_blank" >Trump’s attacks on journalists</a>, threats to sue over coverage he doesn’t like and attempts at turning the press into his personal Pravda won’t convince the soccer mom in Bakersfield, California, that $5 a gallon gas is somehow affordable. We can’t eat censorship.</p><p>Trump’s obsession with baseless election fraud claims and threats to rig or militarize our elections won’t help the recent college grad who’s sent out 300 resumes but can’t get a job. We can’t eat paranoia.</p><p>Trump’s preoccupation with authoritarian strongmen like Russia’s Vladimir Putin, China’s Xi Jinping and North Korea’s Kim Jong Un is a slap in the face of a Cuban refugee trying to make a life for his family in Miami. We can’t eat jealousy.</p><p>Running the country in service of one guy’s megalomania hasn’t made America great again, and it hasn’t made life better for Americans.</p><p>We can’t eat Trump.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-870000" name="module-870000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Expand Smart Streets program citywide to enhance safety
entries.summary: <p>On Friday, less than a week after yet <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/10/04/cyclist-fatally-hit-driver-east-garfield-park" >another cyclist’s death</a> over the weekend, the City Council’s <a class="Link" href="https://occprodstoragev1.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/meetingattachmentspublic/57db25a7-6e4d-40ac-9843-e8ad10c8a4bb.pdf" target="_blank" >Committee on Pedestrian and Traffic Safety</a> will have an opportunity to expand one of Chicago’s most promising tools for changing dangerous driving behavior — the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2024/11/04/smart-streets-bus-bike-lane-ticket" >Smart Streets</a> program.</p><p>I like that the Smart Streets program is designed specifically to be about changing behavior, not money. People receive warnings first. This is to tell people: “We haven’t been caring about this, but we’re going to now.” Blocking a bike lane, parking at a bus stop or double parking with the flashers on “just to run in real quick” is not going to be something that's allowed anymore.</p><p>And it works. The city’s own data shows that 84% of drivers who received a zero-dollar warning did not go on to receive a fine. And 64% of drivers who received one ticket did not reoffend.</p><p>The pilot has demonstrated that this approach can change behavior. We should build on that success and make Smart Streets permanent citywide.</p><p><i>Cyrus Dowlatshahi, Humboldt Park</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-000000" name="module-000000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Establish term limits in Highland Park </h3><p>In less than a month, Highland Park residents will be asked to consider a <a class="Link" href="https://www.cityhpil.com/government/city_departments/city_managers_office/city_clerk/term_limits.php" target="_blank" >referendum </a>on whether term limits should be imposed on those seeking to run for mayor or the City Council.  Term limits have become a lightning rod of sorts for the electorate, not only on a local level, but for those serving nationally in Congress and the Supreme Court.  </p><p>Certainly there are pros and cons to imposing such limits, but as a 50-year resident of Highland Park, I can say from experience that local politicians who serve, or want to continue to serve, for lengthy periods do so by imperiling progress for the community with outdated notions and policies that once were effective but wane with time. These politicians become "stale."  It is time for a change, and Highland Park residents will have an opportunity to become part of a vanguard with some other municipalities in Lake, DeKalb, Cook and Will counties —including Lake Forest and Wilmette that neighbor Highland Park — by voting for such limits.</p><p><i>Miles Zaremski, Highland Park</i> </p><h3>Toilet talk</h3><p>Oui, oui to public toilets!</p><p>I couldn't agree more with Sun-Times columnist Neil Steinberg that providing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/10/04/public-toilet-chicago-bathroom-desert-paris-london-tourism-steinberg" >public restrooms</a> is a goal worth working toward in Chicago. I am someone who has often found myself in the undignified position of panicking while looking for a restroom. Public facilities would provide locals and visitors alike with dignity while exploring our city.</p><p><i>Robert Scheffel, North Center</i><br></p>
