entries.title: Orthodox church modeled after 15th century monastery heads toward landmark status
entries.summary: <p>St. Simeon Mirotočivi Serbian Orthodox Church is easy to miss for most Chicagoans, owing to the fact that it's tucked away in the far southeast corner of the city — closer to Hammond, Indiana, than say, State and Madison.</p><p>However, those who have seen the church, at 3737 E. 114th St., are unlikely to forget it: a magnificent pile of Byzantine Revival architecture with its crucifix-topped towers and unique two-tone brickwork with an eye-opening array of arches, horizontal stripes and checkerboard patterns.</p><p>The church, which is located in the East Side neighborhood, is likely to get more attention soon. That’s because the edifice is on the road toward receiving city landmark status.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Planning and Development’s Historic Preservation Division recommended St. Simeon and its accompanying Serbian Hall for preliminary landmark status.</p><p>It was before the Commission on Chicago Landmarks on Thursday as part of a brief confirmation that the designation would align with the city's planning goals for the area. The commission could vote on the designation at next month's meeting.</p><p>The congregation supports the designation, landmarks officials said.</p><p>Landmark status would be a great win for the community and the Far Southeast Side, a part of town better known for surviving the 1970s and 1980s crash of the steel industry than for good architecture.</p><p>And if any church deserves it, it's St. Simeon.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-6b0000" name="image-6b0000"></a> <picture entries.title: To protect immigrant students, a Chicago-area college told Flock to remove its cameras. The company refused.
entries.summary: <p>When Elgin Community College hired Flock Safety to install six surveillance cameras in April 2025, President Peggy Heinrich thought they would “enhance the safety and security of students.”</p><p>The company’s automatic license plate readers use artificial intelligence to track the registration, model and details like dents and bumper stickers of every passing vehicle. They were supposed to help locate stolen cars and missing people.</p><p>But Heinrich started to wonder if the cameras were actually making students less safe after seeing news reports that data captured by Flock cameras in Illinois had been <a class="Link" href="https://www.nprillinois.org/illinois/2025-08-27/hundreds-of-police-departments-use-camera-company-accused-of-breaking-state-law" target="_blank" ><u>shared with U.S. Customs and Border Protection</u>.</a> Then in September 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement <a class="Link" href="https://elgin.edu/news/ecc-in-the-news/2025/reported-ice-activity-on-campus.php" target="_blank" ><u>detained an Elgin Community College student</u></a> in a campus parking lot.</p><p>More than half of students at the far west suburban Chicago campus identify as Latino. Heinrich said enrollment dipped. Students were afraid to come to class. College officials decided the cameras had to go.</p><p>“We're just doing everything we can here to be sure this feels like a safe place for our students to come,” Heinrich said. “We want them to come here and to be able to focus on learning.”</p><p>As concerns about Flock and other makers of automatic license plate readers continue to emerge, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/17/five-public-universities-in-illinois-use-controversial-flock-cameras-to-surveil-campus" target="_blank" ><u>students and educators across Illinois</u></a> are calling on college leaders to terminate their contracts with the company. They say the surveillance technology violates student privacy and endangers immigrant students and student activists who’ve been targeted by the Trump administration.</p><div class="Enhancement" Students have to pass at least one of the college’s seven Flock cameras on their way to class there.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Lisa Kurian Philip/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Public records obtained by surveillance researcher Torin Monahan and WBEZ show that data captured by Flock cameras at other Illinois public campuses, including <a class="Link" href="https://dataverse.unc.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.15139/S3/FDPBPJ" target="_blank" ><u>Joliet Junior College</u></a>, the University of Illinois Chicago and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, was searched dozens of times last year in connection with immigration enforcement. In some cases, federal immigration authorities directly accessed colleges’ data. <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilsos.gov/news/2025/august-25-2025-giannoulias-audit-finds-license-plate-reader-company-in-violation-of-state-law.html" target="_blank" ><u>The Illinois Secretary of State</u></a> also found that U.S. Customs and Border Protection searched Illinois Flock data last year in violation of state law.</p><p>Heinrich said her staff audited the campus’ Flock data and found no evidence to suggest it had been accessed by federal immigration agents. Still, college officials asked Flock to remove the surveillance cameras “out of an abundance of caution for our students,” Heinrich said.</p><p>But getting the cameras taken down was not as simple as it sounds, especially because Flock retains ownership of the company’s equipment. Flock responded to Elgin Community College’s request with silence — and even resistance.</p><p>Flock Safety did not respond to WBEZ’s request for comment. <a class="Link" href="https://www.flocksafety.com/blog/does-flock-share-data-with-ice" target="_blank" ><u>The company has said</u></a> federal agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, can no longer access local Flock data unless law enforcement agencies grant access.</p><p>Surveillance experts say the company is financially incentivized to have as many cameras gathering data as possible even in places that no longer want them, because potential clients are looking for the surveillance network with the greatest reach.</p><p>“You get to access even more cameras throughout the country,” said Monahan, a professor at the University of North Carolina Chapel Hill.</p><p>Elgin Community College staff notified Flock in October 2025 that they wanted to cancel their contract and have the cameras taken down. Within a day, Heinrich said, Flock rejected the request and refused to uninstall the equipment on the basis that the company had not breached their agreement.</p><p>College officials reached out again in December 2025 and said they would pay for the remaining five months of the contract — they just wanted the cameras taken down.</p><p>“We never received a response back from Flock,” Heinrich said.</p><p>That’s when things got weird. Heinrich said Elgin Community College staff began to cover the cameras using black trash bags and zip ties so that they would not be able to capture footage. But workers in an unmarked vehicle, which Heinrich assumed belonged to Flock, repeatedly removed the coverings.</p><p>“We were kind of in a back and forth for a bit where we’d cover, and then when they'd come to service, they'd remove,” Heinrich said. “Then we'd cover and then they'd remove.”</p><p>This strange dance continued, Heinrich said, until Elgin Community College’s contract with Flock expired in April this year and the company uninstalled the cameras for good.</p><h3><b>Flock cameras can undermine efforts to make students feel welcome </b></h3><p>But public records show Flock’s license plate readers are still installed at several other colleges across the state, including at five of the state’s 12 public universities and at four community colleges.</p><p>That’s the case at southwest suburban Joliet Junior College. At the main campus entrance, which is bordered on one side by cornfields, students like Lui Rodriguez have to pass at least one of the college’s seven Flock cameras to get to class.</p><div The 26-year-old said the staff goes to great lengths to make students feel a sense of belonging. Rodriguez has even baked cookies with the dean of students to raise funds for the student group Latinos Unidos.</p><p>“The staff here care about the students,” Rodriguez said.</p><p>So Rodriguez was shocked when he found out that Joliet Junior College contracts with Flock — and that <u>public records show</u> data captured by cameras on campus was directly accessed by federal immigration agents last year.</p><p>“It's kind of like a backstab to the students,” Rodriguez said. “I wish more people knew about it.”</p><p>Katie Smith, a spokesperson for Joliet Junior College, said college leaders and campus police proactively review who has access to their Flock data and would take any misuse of this information seriously. The college’s contract with Flock is up for renewal in July 2027.</p><p>“The College remains committed to fostering a welcoming and inclusive environment for all students and staff while balancing its responsibility to provide a safe campus environment,” Smith said in a written statement. “The safety of our students and the broader campus community is paramount.”</p><p>But Rodriguez said those reassurances, and the Flock cameras, do not make him feel safer on campus.</p><p>“We’re being surveilled and our information can be used to track us down and detain us,” Rodriguez said. “That’s not conducive to education and learning.”</p><p><i>Lisa Kurian Philip covers higher education for WBEZ in partnership with</i> <a class="Link" href="https://www.opencampusmedia.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Open Campus</i></a><i>.</i></p>

entries.title: What’s your NITA dream project? Experts weigh in as new agency directing CTA, Metra, Pace plans budget
entries.summary: <p>Ever dream of a project to improve the city's trains and buses?</p><p>Maybe it's a specific bus lane. Or a new or extended L line. Or a Metra route.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/10/nita-northern-illinois-transit-authority-cta-metra-pace" target="_blank" >Northern Illinois Transit Authority</a> is finalizing its 2027 budget. As the new agency in charge of the CTA, Metra and Pace, NITA is seeking public input to fulfill its goal of transforming public transit into something everyone wants to use.</p><p>The Sun-Times wants to hear how you — our readers — want NITA to spend its nearly $1.5 billion in extra cash.</p><p>Send your recommendations to <a class="Link" href="mailto:dstruett@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >dstruett@suntimes.com</a> or fill out the form below. We plan to publish some of them in the near future.</p><p>Meanwhile, here are the NITA dream projects of some transit experts:</p><h3>More housing near transit hubs</h3><p>"I envision a totally transformed regional housing market that has enough 'transit-oriented' housing options to finally meet the overwhelming demand for families to be able to afford to live and work near a bus or rail station," says <b>Dan Lurie, president and CEO of Metropolitan Planning Council</b>.</p><p><b>Juan Sebastian, executive director of Elevated Chicago</b>, agrees.</p><p>"My dream investment for NITA is creating the nation’s leading equitable transit-oriented development program, helping communities build more affordable homes, local businesses and vibrant public spaces near transit."</p><h3>Bus corridors on Western, Ashland avenues</h3><p>"Chicago is primed and ready to benefit from bus rapid transit on Western Avenue," says <b>Amy Rynell, executive president of the Active Transportation Alliance</b>. "BRT creates a train-like transit experience for a fraction of the cost of heavy rail. Dedicated lanes, pre-paid boarding, train-like stations and smart traffic signals all combine to speed up the bus and provide a fast, reliable and affordable alternative to driving.<i>"</i></p><p>Add Ashland Avenue to the list of north-south roads primed for a dedicated bus corridor, says <b>Andrew Mack, an organizer</b> of the Bridgeport Kidical Mass Family Bike Ride and a founding member of the 11th Ward Safe Streets Union. "It has long been clear that a transportation system based on private cars is a poor plan for moving millions of people around our city. Bus rapid transit lines on Ashland and Western should be fast-tracked by NITA. The city that works needs to also be the city that moves."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" <b>Peter Tucic, vice president of public policy for the Chicago Lighthouse</b>, which advocates for the blind. The idea for crosstown Metra service is called the STAR:Line and has been long promoted by <a class="Link" href="https://buildthetunnelchicago.org/" target="_blank" >a blog promoting #BuildTheTunnel</a>. "Now that NITA exists, we have an opportunity to create real alignment among the region’s three transit systems," Tucic says.</p><p><b>Rick Harnish, executive director of the High Speed Rail Alliance</b>, wants Metra service to be electrified and run more frequently so it's not just for commuters. "That would mean trains departing every 15 minutes or better. Metra Electric, especially the South Chicago Branch, is the best place for an early success."</p><h3>Connect Union Station and Blue Line</h3><p>"Fast-track a high-quality tunnel from Chicago Union Station to the Blue Line's Clinton Station, with prominent signage and, if space allows, a moving sidewalk," says <b>Joseph Schwieterman, director of DePaul University's Chaddick Institute for Metropolitan Development</b>. "This would be an important step toward more fully integrating Metra/Amtrak and CTA rail. The tunnel would also improve access to the Intercity Bus Station, which was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/06/17/greyhound-bus-terminal-flixbus" target="_blank" >purchased by the city in August</a>."</p><h3>Community spaces near L stations</h3><p>NITA should build community spaces near the four proposed Red Line extension stations, says <b>Olatunji Oboi Reed, president and CEO of Equiticity</b>. This nonprofit calls them <a class="Link" href="https://www.equiticity.org/blog/-the-go-hub" target="_blank" >“Go Hubs”</a> — buildings that serve as community spaces where people can get access e-bikes and other ways to complete their trips to and from home. "Our goal is achieving racial equity, mobility justice, environmental justice and community ownership, translating physical mobility into upward social mobility," Reed says.</p><h3>Instead of a dream project, focus on fiscal responsibility</h3><p>"I am looking for NITA to be a good steward of taxpayers’ dollars," says<b> Ian Savage, professor of economics and transportation at Northwestern University</b>. "That means getting the operating agencies to get their existing infrastructure into a state of good repair and ensuring seamless transfers between a coordinated network of bus, L and regional rail services. I think NITA needs to demonstrate operational and fiscal responsibility on existing services before spending public money on expansionist proposals."</p><h3>What do you think?</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-e80000" name="html-embed-module-e80000"></a><div class="contribly-contribute-v2" data-client="b20193c8-5c0c-4a5b-a770-64305c544c4e" data-assignment="c248a6dc-070b-454b-84f6-5ebe9f47009e" data-display="inline" data-language="en-gb"></div><script type="text/javascript" src="https://s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/contribly-widgets/contribute/contribute-v2.5.js"></script> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Demanda de la familia de Silverio Villegas González pide daños y perjuicios por su muerte por ICE
entries.summary: <p>La familia de Silverio Villegas González, el hombre que un agente de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) le disparó y lo mató durante el Operativo Midway Blitz, presentó el jueves una demanda administrativa en busca de una compensación del gobierno federal por su muerte.</p><p>José Villegas González, hermano de Villegas González, presentó la reclamación en virtud de la ley Federal Tort Claims Act en nombre del patrimonio de su hermano, solicitando una compensación por su “muerte injusta”. La reclamación es un paso obligatorio antes de demandar al gobierno federal.</p><p>Jonathan Manes, abogado del MacArthur Justice Center que representa a la familia, dijo que esperan pedir “una suma muy grande de dinero”, aunque no quiso revelar el monto total.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-600000" name="module-600000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La reclamación incluye unos $10,000 por daños al automóvil de Villegas González y a sus pertenencias, aunque eso es aparte de la compensación por el sufrimiento que padeció y por las pérdidas emocionales y económicas de la familia.</p><p>“No estamos enfocados en la cifra en este momento”, dijo Manes. “Se trata de conocer la verdad y de exigir responsabilidades por lo que le pasó a Silverio”.</p><p>La demanda alega que dos agentes de ICE crearon una confrontación peligrosa y le dispararon a Villegas González cuando pudieron haberse apartado de su automóvil. También acusa a ICE y a funcionarios del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) de no haber capacitado ni supervisado adecuadamente a sus agentes.</p><p>Villegas González, de 38 años, había emigrado de México y vivió en Estados Unidos durante unos 18 años antes de morir. Trabajaba como cocinero y criaba a dos hijos.</p><p>Había dejado a sus hijos en la escuela y en la guardería y se dirigía al trabajo el 12 de septiembre de 2025, cuando los dos agentes de ICE intentaron detener su automóvil en Franklin Park y uno de ellos le disparó a Villegas González. Más tarde murió en el Loyola University Medical Center.</p><p>Después del tiroteo, DHS dijo que Villegas González había huido de una parada de tránsito y había arrastrado a un agente “una distancia considerable”. El departamento dijo que el agente resultó gravemente herido y abrió fuego porque temía por su vida.</p><p>Pero imágenes de la cámara corporal de la policía obtenidas por el Chicago Sun-Times mostraron al agente describiendo sus lesiones como “nada grave”. Su compañero informó una lesión en la rodilla y cortes en las manos.</p><p>La denuncia presentada por la familia de Villegas González se basa en video de vigilancia, grabaciones policiales e informes de ambulancia y de autopsia para cuestionar la versión del gobierno.</p><p>Manes dijo que el gobierno defendió el tiroteo antes de que pudiera investigar lo ocurrido.</p><p>“Ese mismo día en que mataron a Silverio, antes de que pudiera haber cualquier tipo de investigación, ya lo estaban calificando como justificado”, dijo.</p><p>Cuando Villegas González intentó alejarse conduciendo, el agente del lado del conductor de su automóvil se aferró a la ventana en lugar de apartarse, dijo Manes.</p><p>“No está en el camino del vehículo”, dijo Manes. “Y dispararle a Silverio no hace más que matarlo y dejar el carro completamente fuera de control”.</p><p>“La política de DHS confirma que no se le puede disparar a una persona solo porque se está alejando manejando”, añadió.</p><p>José Villegas González busca una compensación en nombre del patrimonio de su hermano por el dolor y sufrimiento antes de morir y por el “sufrimiento mental” de la familia, incluida la pérdida por parte de sus hijos del apoyo “emocional” y “económico” de su padre, según la denuncia.</p><p>Manes dijo que Villegas González tuvo dificultades para respirar y seguir con vida después de recibir un disparo en el cuello.</p><p>La compensación beneficiaría a los hijos y al cónyuge de Villegas González, no a su hermano, dijo Manes. La reclamación describe a Villegas González como el principal cuidador de sus hijos. Después de su muerte, los niños fueron colocados en un hogar de acogida en Idaho, lejos de sus familiares en el área de Chicago.</p><p>DHS dijo al Sun-Times en julio que los fiscales federales decidieron no presentar cargos contra el agente que le disparó y mató a Villegas González. Los funcionarios federales aún no han explicado públicamente por qué. Manes dijo que la familia no ha recibido un informe del incidente ni los nombres de los agentes involucrados.</p><p>La denuncia alega que el FBI tomó el control de la investigación poco después del tiroteo, pero no llevó a cabo una investigación adecuada.</p><p>En un comunicado, el FBI dijo que “respondió al incidente en Franklin Park y brindó asistencia a las autoridades en el lugar”, pero se negó a confirmar o negar si existe una investigación, citando la política del Departamento de Justicia (DOJ).</p><p>Franklin Park esperó más de siete meses para pedir a la Policía Estatal de Illinois que investigara, y lo hizo el mismo día en que la Comisión de Responsabilidad de Illinois publicó un informe demoledor sobre Midway Blitz.</p><p>La investigación estatal sigue abierta.</p><p>“Un año no ha borrado ni disminuido el dolor que sentimos por su ausencia”, dijeron José Villegas González y su esposa, Ana Villegas, en un comunicado en septiembre.</p><p>La demanda por daños y perjuicios le da a DHS y al FBI la oportunidad de revisar las acusaciones y considerar un acuerdo. Si el gobierno la rechaza o no toma una decisión final en un plazo de seis meses, la familia puede seguir adelante con una demanda.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Suspects in Englewood CTA bus shooting that left passengers, 57 and 65, injured due in court
entries.summary: <p>A man and a woman have been charged with a shooting aboard a CTA bus sparked over a seat last week that left bystanders 57 and 65 wounded late last month in Englewood.</p><p>Tyrese Jones, 19, and Destiny Jones, 18, were charged with attempted murder, aggravated battery and aggravated battery to a transit passenger, police said. <br>The two were scheduled for a detention hearing Friday at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse. It was unclear if they are related. </p><p>Tyrese Jones, of Mundelein, and Destiny Jones is of the Grand Boulevard neighborhood. </p><p>They were identified as the people who, on Sept. 30, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/30/2-hospitalized-after-being-hit-by-gunfire-while-on-cta-bus" target="_blank" >allegedly participated in shooting </a>and seriously injuring a 57-year-old man and a 65-year-old woman, both of whom were passengers aboard the CTA bus in the 300 block of West 63rd Street, police said. </p><p>An <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/03/aspiring-paramedic-recalls-how-a-cta-bus-seat-dispute-turned-into-shooting" target="_blank" >aspiring paramedic who witnessed the attack</a> told the Sun-Times he was on his way home from work when a man and woman began fighting with another passenger over a wet seat, according to the witness and police reports obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><p>“Basically, the lady wanted him to get up, and he didn’t want to get up, so she apparently got to swinging on him,” the witness said.</p><p>When the argument turned physical, the seated passenger reportedly pulled a gun and fired, authorities said.</p>

entries.title: Feds appear to hide name of government lawyer in new 'Broadview Six' court filings
entries.summary: <p>Federal prosecutors in Chicago appeared<b> </b>Friday<b> </b>to be hiding the name of an attorney representing<b> </b>the United States government<b> </b>in the ongoing legal fight over the doomed "Broadview Six" case, originally brought against six Operation Midway Blitz protesters.</p><p>U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros' office filed<b> </b>two<b> </b>partially redacted documents overnight<b>, </b>seeking U.S. District Judge April<b> </b>Perry's permission<b> </b>to disclose grand jury transcripts<b> </b>and<b> </b>exhibits. It cited the Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure requiring grand jury secrecy<b> </b>as one reason to hide portions of the documents from the public.</p><p>The documents were filed by Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas<b> </b>Walsh, the head of Boutros' civil division. But the feds made the unusual move of covering up what appeared to be the signature block of a second attorney representing the U.S. government.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/01/broadview-six-perry-boutros-mecklenburg" >‘Broadview Six’ judge wants to put prosecutors under oath, keeps contempt charges on the table</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Representatives of Boutros' office and the Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday morning. Grand jury transcripts in the case have already been made public, something Perry noted on the court docket after Boutros' request was apparently first made under seal earlier this week. </p><p>It is highly unusual for the name of a government attorney to be redacted from such a document. Even in the Chicago prosecution of violent Sinaloa cartel figures, the names of Justice Department attorneys appear on the public record, along with their professional contact information.</p><p>It's particularly striking in the "Broadview Six" case, in which Boutros' office has already been accused of a cover-up. </p><p>Perry <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/01/broadview-six-perry-boutros-mecklenburg" target="_blank" >announced last week</a> that<b> </b>further<b> </b>“under oath”<b> </b>fact-finding is necessary in the tainted case. In doing so, she left open the possibility of naming a special prosecutor<b> </b>to investigate Boutros and other Justice Department officials.</p><p>That means the threat of a criminal investigation continues to hang over what was once seen as a top-tier U.S. attorney’s office, where the mantra has long been “do the right thing.”</p><p>Perry announced her intention at the end of an hourlong hearing<b> </b>in which she asked an attorney for Boutros’ office whether any of the prosecutors who worked on the politically charged “Broadview Six” case would invoke their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.</p><p>He didn’t rule it out.</p><p>Perry told the lawyers, “My sole focus, at this point, is on lack of candor, concealment of material facts, or other misconduct that occurred before me.” The comment was likely designed to avoid separation-of-powers concerns from derailing her inquiry.</p><p>The “Broadview Six” case revolved around a protest outside an immigration holding facility in west suburban Broadview in September 2025. Prosecutors alleged that a crowd pushed and damaged a federal agent’s SUV.</p><p>But from that crowd, only six people were charged with a conspiracy to impede the agent. Most of them were involved in local Democratic politics.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Charged were then-congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, then-Cook County Board candidate Catherine “Cat” Sharp, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt, musician<b> </b>Joselyn<b> </b>Walsh<b> </b>and<b> </b>Abughazaleh<b> </b>campaign<b> </b>worker<b> </b>Andre Martin.</p><p>The case against them collapsed on May 21, after Perry alleged that Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri<b> </b>Mecklenburg spoke to grand jurors outside the grand jury room and put her personal credibility on the line to support charges. The judge also indicated Mecklenburg had excused grand jurors who disagreed with the feds’ case, a claim Mecklenburg denies.</p><p>Mecklenburg recently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/09/24/broadview-six-sheri-mecklenburg" target="_blank" >retired from the Justice Department</a> in order to defend herself, insisting that she followed the instructions of Boutros’ front office<b> </b>“at every turn.”</p><p>But Perry said she found “most problematic” the fact that the apparent misconduct was redacted out of transcripts initially given to her by Boutros’ office. The redactions were made after Mecklenburg withdrew from the case.</p>

entries.title: Cubs’ Matt Shaw among featured speakers at conservative political event later this year
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> utility man Matt Shaw is listed among the featured speakers at a conservative political event in December.</p><p>The event, hosted by Turning Point USA – the group founded by controversial podcaster and influencer Charlie Kirk, who was shot and killed last year – features many other political and media figures associated with President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement, including Vice President JD Vance and Donald Trump Jr.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">The first speaker drop of AmericaFest 2026 is HERE 🔥<br><br>Restore the culture. Reclaim America.<br><br>Be there: <a href="https://t.co/kMi2p7BBuS">https://t.co/kMi2p7BBuS</a> <a href="https://t.co/L5OJtsGL4S">pic.twitter.com/L5OJtsGL4S</a></p>— Turning Point USA (@TPUSA) <a href="https://x.com/TPUSA/status/2108256133593104463?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 8, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Shaw, who notably <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/09/21/cubs-third-baseman-matt-shaw-leaves-team-to-attend-charlie-kirk-memorial-service" >left the Cubs to attend Kirk’s memorial service</a> last September, became friends with Kirk, an Arlington Heights native, while the two lived in the same apartment complex in Arizona.</p><p>“The reason Charlie and I connected so close was because of our faith,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/09/23/cubs-matt-shaw-charlie-kirk-memorial-leaving-team-meant-to-be" >Shaw said after returning to the team</a> last season. “That’s something that drives me every single day, something that I think about all the time.</p><p>“So if people are wondering who I am and what I stand for, I’d say that my faith and the many blessings I’ve been given is why I’m able to be here. And I just want to make sure that I can give that back to people, that I can support people around me, that I can love people around me the same way that I’ve been blessed.”</p><p>Shaw was the Cubs’ everyday third baseman during the 2025 season, but he was relegated to a bench role after the team signed two-time World Series champion Alex Bregman to a free-agent contract last offseason.</p><p>Some of Shaw’s offensive numbers improved this season, though that came in limited time, with multiple injuries keeping him to just 77 games.</p><p>Whether Shaw, who appeared in 34 games in the outfield during the 2026 season, factors more heavily into <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/10/03/four-offseason-questions-facing-jed-hoyer-cubs-who-have-pitching-at-top-of-lengthy-to-do-list" >the Cubs’ plans for 2027</a> remains to be seen. The team could be searching to fill two holes in the outfield, with left fielder Ian Happ and right fielder Seiya Suzuki slated to hit free agency.</p><p>Team president Jed Hoyer said last week that both Shaw and fellow reserve infielder Pedro Ramirez could play larger roles in the future.</p><p>“Having Pedro and Matt, super versatile, both really good players, we can ask more of them going forward,” Hoyer said. “We didn’t have to this year, given the nature of our corner outfield. But I think they both can certainly do that, and we’ll lean on both those guys more heavily going forward.”</p>
